articles.title: Spec-Driven UI Component Development
articles.thesis: Curtis argues that component specs should be the central record of design intent. Specs collect intent from several places where it starts (Figma, prototypes, code), store it in normalised, versioned form, and pass it back out to each of those places. Specs should be generated by deterministic transforms wherever possible, with authored requirements covering only what tools cannot express. A schema turns spec content into a contract, so consumers can build predictably and every change can be classed as breaking, minor or patch. Code factories, not docs, are the main consumers.

spec_structure.what_it_holds: The component's name, its props and its named elements: the public surface used to configure and override it.
spec_structure.quote: API declares component names, props and elements

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Layered, cascading rules (like CSS) for styles, tokens, prop bindings, slots, composition, layout and structure, per variant. He says this data is rich and complex, and for now is best authored only in Figma.
spec_structure.quote: Variants declare layered rules (much like CSS)

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Composed instances with nested slots, content and images. They are reused for docs, test cases and scaffolds.
spec_structure.quote: Examples carries composed relationships via nested slots, content, and images

spec_structure.what_it_holds: The component's named elements. He shows it only as a path in the versioning rules, component.anatomy.element: adding an element counts as a minor change.
spec_structure.quote: Add a <component name>.anatomy.<element name>? Minor.

spec_structure.what_it_holds: The component's props. He shows it only as a path in the versioning rules, component.props.prop: changing or removing a prop is a breaking change. The article gives no typing or default syntax.
spec_structure.quote: Change or remove <component name>.props.<prop name>? Breaking!

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Markdown files kept in the specs repo for intent that Figma cannot express: behaviour, accessibility, motion, advanced configurations such as discriminated unions and prop relationships, and cross-component rules such as disabled taking precedence over read-only. Files can be general (for example configurations.md) or scoped to a component and platform (for example card.accessibility.android.md). Requirements use MUST, SHOULD and COULD wording.
spec_structure.quote: teams augment generated specs with authored supplemental requirements

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Tokens, fonts, icons, images and other product marks and assets that sit alongside the component specs. Formats vary by enterprise, and he leaves taxonomy for another post.
spec_structure.quote: components are served by foundations that include tokens, fonts, icons

spec_structure.section_or_field: Versions with changelog and release notes
spec_structure.what_it_holds: Each specs version comes with change logs, change sets and release notes written with a skill. They answer two questions: are these the changes we want, and what is different for consumers.
spec_structure.quote: Each version is accompanied by change logs, change sets

spec_structure.what_it_holds: The explicit structure for all specs content. Schema plus content together form the contract. Validating against the schema lets each change be classified objectively as major, minor or patch.
spec_structure.quote: Combining a schema with the content we put in it forms a contract

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Architecture decision records that evolve the schema and tools. Their sections are metadata, context, problem, alternatives, decision, consequences and other concerns.
spec_structure.quote: record decisions in a format with structured sections

spec_structure.what_it_holds: The status that bulk commands look for in a Figma file to decide which components to generate specs for.
spec_structure.quote: scan for components marked READY_FOR_DEV

examples: A figure (shown only as an image, caption only seen) of generated per-component spec files: one component's specs split into API, variants and examples files.

A figure of supplemental requirements files: general files such as a configurations Markdown file next to component-, concern- and platform-scoped files named in a component.concern.platform.md pattern (for example card, accessibility, android).
A figure of one design system's folder with tokens and assets beside the component specs.

Three inline versioning rules that use dotted paths into the spec: component.props.prop (change or remove means breaking), component.anatomy.element (add means minor), and a token rebound on an element within one variant (patch).
A list of the sections an ADR contains: metadata, context, problem, alternatives, decision, consequences, other concerns.

Three example analysis questions answered by generated reports: where one text token is used across components and elements, how state options vary across components, and which components a change to the icon component's API would affect.

rules.rule: Prefer specs generated by deterministic transforms over hand-authored ones, and over time build tools that move more of the spec into generated form.
Pair generated specs with authored requirements for whatever the design tool cannot express: behaviour, accessibility, motion, discriminated unions and prop relationships.
Store authored requirements as files in the specs repo, scoped as general, per component, per concern and per platform, so agents and scripts can find and filter them.
Write requirements in a consistent format with MUST, SHOULD and COULD levels, and use skills to keep the wording tight. Changes go in by pull request for teammates to review and approve.
Write cross-component state rules as general requirements. His example: disabled takes precedence over read-only.
Different paths that produce specs (Plugin API, REST API) must give byte-identical output. Keep that true with fixtures, harnesses and loops.
Render specs back into Figma with a deterministic script, not agent inference. Prove the transform is lossless with round trips (specs to Figma to specs, byte-identical).

A transform command turns specs into CSS, a TypeScript contract, a React component scaffold and Storybook stories. It relies on Figma authoring conventions for states and for component- and element-specific roles to generate behaviour.
Generated code is a prototype or starting point, not production code. Engineers' factories and per-platform skills harden it.
To bring prototype code back into specs, keep spec-generated choices separate from platform-specific code, for example in separate generated, extensions and overrides stylesheets.
Transforms must be lossless, cheap and fast in every direction before cross-surface synchronisation is attempted.
Use the schema to classify each change mechanically: removing or changing a prop is major, adding an anatomy element is minor, rebinding a token in one variant is a patch.
Evolve the schema, tools and conventions through ADRs. Use an LLM to explore alternatives from the ADR as the baseline, then let humans review the familiar format.
Generate analysis reports every release from spec data (token and style usage, prop models, dependencies, key naming) so questions are answered by data rather than ad-hoc extraction.
Downstream code factories compare spec-derived CSS, contracts and TSX against existing code, and testing turns spec variants, content and examples into tests for designer review.
Changes engineers make to API, accessibility and behaviour count as design intent and should flow back upstream into requirements and the schema.

Do not generate usage docs from specs. Prop tables and how-to-use content come from the coded implementations, and artwork from Figma. Specs record names and changes, and cover how to build a component well.

terms.meaning: Structured, versioned data that describes a component as completely as possible. It acts as the hub of design intent across Figma, prototypes, code and docs.
The several surfaces where intent may start (Figma, prototypes, code). Specs normalise, synchronise and version them, rather than being one single source of truth.
Generated specs are deterministic extractions, for example from Figma. Authored specs are requirements written by humans or agents for what extraction cannot capture.
Authored Markdown requirement files, general or scoped to a component, concern and platform.
The schema combined with the spec content. Consumers build against it predictably and absorb changes gradually.
Specs to Figma and back to specs, with a byte-identical result. It proves a transform loses nothing.
Identical output from different generation paths, here the Plugin API and the REST API.
An engineering subsystem that turns spec data into platform code and compares it with existing code.
Architecture decision record, used to evolve the schema, tools and conventions.
The author's role of routing upstream requests from factories and workflows to the right owner.
The Figma status that bulk spec generation filters on.

warnings: Figma cannot express behaviour, accessibility, advanced layout, or configurations such as discriminated unions and prop relationships. Generated specs alone are incomplete.
Motion is still expressed through prototypes plus written requirements, not in the spec data itself.
Using agent inference to render specs costs money and risks loss and imprecision, because spec data is layered and complex. Deterministic scripts avoid this.
The Figma Plugin API and REST API differ. Keeping their outputs identical takes ongoing work (skills, fixtures, harnesses).
Extracting specs from prototype code is early and hard, especially the layout tree.
Synchronisation across surfaces cannot be attempted until every transform is lossless, cheap and fast.
The edges between tools and teams are where things get hard: no one person owns the whole pipeline, and the edges must be agreed.
Generated prototype code is not production-ready.
Specs contribute little to usage docs. Prop tables and how-to-use content belong to code implementations and a separate docs team.

Engineers fill behaviour and accessibility gaps that designers missed, which pushes the schema to model richer prop patterns, composition, behaviours and accessibility. He describes some parts of the system as still leaking.
gaps: The article does not give the spec's field-level schema. It names three generated files (API, variants, examples) and two dotted paths (props, anatomy), and points to a separate post and the author's published schema for details. Neither was read here.
It does not say how states are encoded, beyond saying the transform uses Figma authoring conventions for states and that state options vary across components.
It does not say how props are typed or given defaults. Only discriminated unions and prop relationships are named, as things Figma cannot express.
It does not say how parts get roles, beyond component- and element-specific roles taken from Figma conventions and used to generate behaviour.
It gives no token-reference syntax and no layering rules for tokens. Tokens appear only as bindings inside variants and as foundations.
It gives no accessibility structure beyond authored requirement files scoped by component, concern and platform.
Figures were images. Only their captions were read, so any structure shown inside them is not reported.

Tools named: the Specs 2 Figma plugin, a specs command-line tool (with generate, render, transform and analyze commands), the Figma Plugin and REST APIs, GitHub Actions, Storybook, React and TypeScript, and agent skills. None was examined.
The ADR examples on layout positioning, and on sides and corners, are linked but were not read.

articles.title: Component Contracts and Schemas
articles.thesis: A UI component spec should be a contract: a formal, platform-neutral artifact that every implementation (React, iOS, Android, Web Components, Figma) must honour, and that a machine can check. The contract is written against a separately versioned schema that defines what any spec may say. Strict, typed, normalized specs allow deterministic generation of 80-90% of the code before agents step in, cheap regeneration, and governed evolution through ADRs. Loose markdown informs but cannot settle disputes.

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Root type of the schema. A component owns Props, Variants, Elements and Styles.
spec_structure.quote: A Component has Props, including an EnumProp

spec_structure.what_it_holds: The component API. Each prop is typed (string, number, boolean, enum, image, and others), has a name and legal options, and one option is marked as the default.
spec_structure.quote: one of which is the default (like medium)

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Value type, a fixed list of legal values, and the default value. Example: size is an enum of small, medium and large, with medium as the default.
spec_structure.quote: A size enum reduces any possible size to three legal choices.

spec_structure.what_it_holds: A layered, compact list of variant entries. Each entry pairs a configuration (prop or state values such as disabled: true) with only the element style overrides that change. The author says this is closer to CSS than to Figma's full combinatorial variant matrix.
spec_structure.quote: state this as a configuration variant, specifying an opacity of the root element once

spec_structure.what_it_holds: The prop or state values a variant applies to, for example disabled true. This is how states are expressed: as explicit configurations, not as suffixes in names.
spec_structure.quote: configurations: disabled: true

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Named parts (anatomy), such as root, with the style values that apply to that part under that configuration.
spec_structure.quote: An Element is included in a Variant and is bound to Styles

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Style bindings that depend on the element's kind. Containers get backgroundColor and itemSpacing. Text gets textColor as a themed token and typography.fontSize. Glyphs get an icon glyph name. The schema forbids invalid combinations.
spec_structure.quote: No text element should have a backgroundColor

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Templated table sections in less formal markdown specs. He cites Layout, Props and Anatomy as the usual sections. The Specs layout follows the Figma layer hierarchy, which he admits is a bias.
spec_structure.quote: a markdown file with tables for Layout, Props and Anatomy

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Padding, strokeWeight and absolutely positioned elements use start and end, not left and right. Positioning is expressed as edges, not as Figma constraints.
spec_structure.quote: as start and end rather than the familiar left and right

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Content Figma cannot express. Designers add it in an agentic pass after a component is marked READY_FOR_DEV. No field-level structure is given.
spec_structure.quote: compose the behaviors and accessibility Figma can't

spec_structure.what_it_holds: References to other components and glyphs. They must resolve, or the spec is invalid. They are added onto Figma's model through naming conventions.
spec_structure.quote: references a dependency that doesn't exist

spec_structure.what_it_holds: A later schema feature, added through an ADR. It touches the API (a new image prop type), style bindings (backgroundImage), examples and storage.
spec_structure.quote: a new image prop type

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Listed among the parts of the schema surface that the images change affected. Not defined further.
spec_structure.quote: examples and even storage

spec_structure.what_it_holds: The model (the schema) and the content (each spec) are versioned separately. An implementation depends on both.
spec_structure.quote: the schema model ... is versioned too, separately

spec_structure.what_it_holds: A readiness marker on the Figma component that triggers spec generation.
spec_structure.quote: Designers simply mark a component READY_FOR_DEV

examples: A YAML props block. The top-level key is props, with one key per prop name (size). Under it: type (string), enum (a list of three string values: small, medium, large) and default (a scalar string: medium). It shows a prop that is typed, has a fixed set of options and has a default.

A YAML variants block for a disabled state. The top-level key is the component name (button). Under it, variants is a list. Each entry has configurations (a map from prop or state to value, here disabled: true) and elements (a map from part name, root, to style properties, here opacity as a decimal 0.36). It shows one state stated once as an override, compared with Figma, which needs about 96 duplicate variants for the same thing.

A counter-example in prose: one markdown file gives a colour token one hex value in its prose and a different hex value in a YAML inventory, which shows how redundancy lets the spec contradict itself.

rules.rule: Treat the spec as a contract that settles disputes between all implementing platforms, Figma included. No platform owns it.
Keep the schema (what any spec may say) separate from the spec (what a given component says), and version the two independently.
Type every value. Use enums for closed sets, numbers and booleans where they fit, and declare a default for each prop, so that malformed values cannot be written.
Express states and variants as explicit configuration objects, not by naming conventions such as button-primary-hover in token or variant names.
Restrict style properties by element kind: containers, text and glyphs each have their own legal set, for example text gets textColor and typography, never backgroundColor.
State each decision once. A state such as disabled is a single override on the root element, not repeated across every variant combination.
Never record the same value in two places, such as prose and a data inventory. Avoid the redundancy instead of writing rules to keep the copies in sync.
Use platform-neutral terms: start and end instead of left and right, edges instead of Figma constraints. Re-type Figma text props as numbers where the default is numeric.
Override what Figma generates with authored definitions where Figma's prop types are too limited, for example richer props.
Make specs machine-verifiable at two levels: is the spec structurally valid, and does the implementation match it. Reject unknown dependencies, unsupported properties and glyphs that do not exist.
Delete or replace unverifiable load-bearing prose (for example 'tonal layers rather than heavy shadows') with modelled values.
Generation must be deterministic: running it twice with no changes gives an empty diff, and one change shows up as one small additive diff.
Use only inference that is configured by convention, which he calls 'inference I configure', not open-ended LLM interpretation. Agents work on the last stretch, not the foundation.
Generate CSS, stories, TypeScript contracts and scaffolds from the contract with scripts. He says this produces 80-90% of the code before agents are involved.
Keep the cost of updating the contract near zero. Re-fetch and regenerate through a CLI, possibly triggered by a watcher on the main branch of the Figma library.
Pass the validated spec data downstream unchanged. Do not hand consumers markdown that an LLM has smoothed or elaborated.
Make schema changes through ADRs. ADRs drive new schema versions, keep existing specs valid, and let downstream consumers opt in when they are ready.
WCAG contrast and broken links can be linted even in loose formats. Strict structure is what makes other kinds of malformation detectable.

terms.meaning: An artifact that holds a component's design intent in one place so that it can be implemented, verified and evolved across platforms. It settles disputes, unlike a description, which only informs.
The model a contract is written in: types, hierarchy and relationships. It says nothing about any particular component and defines what a contract can say.
An instance written against the schema that states what a particular contract does say, for example that Button has a size prop.
The author's own Figma plugin and command-line tool, with a schema, used to fetch and generate component specs from Figma.
A schema prop type with a name, a list of string options and a default.
A layered override: a configuration of prop or state values plus style changes for each element (part).
A named part inside a variant (for example root), bound to styles that depend on its kind (container, text, glyph).
A definition extracted unchanged from one party's point of view, such as Figma. He says it is not a contract.
Architectural decision record, the mechanism for evolving the schema. He names Sides, Positioning, Numbers and Images ADRs.
A status a designer sets on a Figma component to trigger spec generation.
A contract that is no longer accurate because it costs too much to maintain. He calls it worse than having no contract, because people trust it.

warnings: Markdown specs are loosely structured and not validated, so they cannot settle disputes or be verified. Any text is accepted, for example 'size: med' or 'kind of large'.
Encoding states in naming conventions (hover or active suffixes) means the contract cannot hold implementations to account.
Figma's data model is redundant. A disabled state on a 96-variant button needs 96 more variants, roughly 500 layers.
A spec that records a decision in two places can contradict itself. Do not trust a 'single source of truth' that does this.

Figma bias leaks in. INSTANCE_SWAP prop types, constraint-based positioning and string-typed text props are examples. A platform-neutral hierarchy across platforms is not achievable for now, and his own layout still follows Figma's layer tree.
The name 'Variants' is Figma-biased even though the model behind it is closer to CSS. He accepts this.
Load-bearing prose that cannot be verified is a defect.
LLM smoothing between the validated extract and its consumers throws away the verification. Consumers end up inferring from inference.
Using markdown plus skills and rules as the whole system lets agents introduce uncertainty upstream, where errors harden.
A contract that is expensive to maintain will rot, and a rotted contract is worse than none. Strict tooling is not worth it for about 25 components on one platform.
Changing the contract without governance (for example, notes added to markdown) is drift dressed up as flexibility.
Behaviour and accessibility cannot be extracted from Figma. They are added in a separate agentic pass, and the article gives them no schema detail.
gaps: Every heading is covered: the intro, The Contract, The Schema Shaping the Contract, What makes a good contract and schema, and principles 1 to 7, plus the closing.

The article does not give a full schema. Accessibility, behaviours (keyboard, focus, interaction), content guidelines and part roles (ARIA roles) are named only as things designers add after extraction from Figma, with no fields.
It does not show how interactive states such as hover, focus and pressed are keyed. Only disabled is shown, as a configuration, though configurations clearly generalise to them.
There is no detail on token references in styles beyond 'textColor as a themed token', and no detail on slots or subcomponent composition.
Output targets are named (CSS, stories, TypeScript contracts, scaffolds), but no generator code or file layout is given, apart from a variants.yaml output file.
The linked Specs schema, PJ Onori's Design System Doc spec and the ADRs were not fetched.
No text in the page tried to instruct an agent.

articles.title: Generating Code from Figma via Specs (subtitle: Automating a prototyping kit started a path to shaping behavior and accessibility)
articles.thesis: Component code for a prototyping kit need not be hand-built one component at a time: it can be generated deterministically, in seconds, from expressive component specs extracted from Figma. Writing generators forces gaps in the spec format into the open, and cheaply authored annotations (state mappings, element roles, primitive-to-component mappings) add behaviour and accessibility. Any factory, scripted or agentic, should key off what the spec declares (the contract), never one library's quirks (the catalog).

spec_structure.what_it_holds: One enum per multi-value prop, an interface that uses those enums, and a constant holding the defaults. This is how props are typed and given defaults.
spec_structure.quote: one enum per multi-value prop, an interface that uses them, and a defaults constant

spec_structure.what_it_holds: The renderable component. Engineers or agents duplicate and evolve it rather than editing the generated file.
spec_structure.quote: they'd duplicate and evolve it from here

spec_structure.what_it_holds: CSS for the default and each variant configuration, aware of the state machine and of invalid prop combinations.
spec_structure.quote: sensitive to state machine, invalid prop combinations

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Storybook stories: variants, ready-made examples and a sticker sheet.
spec_structure.quote: including variants, ready-made examples and a sticker sheet

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Each subcomponent gets the same file set (scaffold, contract, metadata, styles, stories) nested under its parent component.
spec_structure.quote: Every component (and related subcomponents) are published to a folder

spec_structure.section_or_field: web components extras: api.ts, metadata.ts, host.css, light.css
spec_structure.what_it_holds: Extra files the web-components generator may add for its own concerns. Their contents are not described.
spec_structure.quote: may layer additional files like api.ts, metadata.ts, host.css and light.css

spec_structure.what_it_holds: A shared runtime file at the root of the generated source. Its contents are not described; the sample code calls helpers such as definedProps, restProps and glyphUrl.
spec_structure.quote: _runtime.ts

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Icons as SVG, images as PNG, fonts the user supplies, plus library-wide tokens emitted as cssvars.css and modes.json.
spec_structure.quote: library-wide tokens are added as cssvars.css and modes

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Maps library-wide state concepts (hover, active, disabled) to the Figma prop and value that express each one, e.g. active = prop state, value pressed; disabled = boolean prop isDisabled.
spec_structure.quote: a mapping of Figma props and enums (like state:rest|hover|pressed) to concepts

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Declares the interaction meaning of one anatomy element (the button, the checkbox control, the label for a control). Added as a role:<role> annotation in Figma or directly in the spec.
spec_structure.quote: A role declares the interaction semantic of an anatomy element

spec_structure.what_it_holds: For each core component (e.g. Text): the Figma layer type it replaces, plus a list of sources (typography style, fill colour, horizontal sizing, content) each mapping Figma values to that component's prop values. The library owner maintains it.
spec_structure.quote: a well-defined mapping maintained by the Figma library owner

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Specs name anatomy elements, and generated markup tags each one with a data-element attribute (root, label, icon, hover). The article assumes these exist but does not describe the anatomy schema itself.
spec_structure.quote: each transform deterministically emits the platform's native control

examples: Directory tree of the React output: a src folder holding a shared runtime file and a components folder. Each component folder holds scaffold, contract, styles and stories files, plus nested subcomponent folders that hold the same files and a metadata file.

Directory tree of assets: icons (SVG, from the fetch command), images (PNG, from the generate command), fonts (user-supplied), and a cssvars folder with a CSS custom-properties file and a modes JSON file, both new and output by the react command.

YAML states mapping: a top-level states key whose children are concept names (hover, active, disabled). Each concept holds a prop name (string) and an optional value (string). Disabled has a prop only, so it maps to a boolean prop.

Generated CSS for the hover variant: a selector combining the component class with :hover, excluding :disabled and aria-disabled true, setting background to a semantic colour custom property. A second rule styles the label element inside it in the same state.

Generated React FavoriteButton scaffold: merges defaults with the props passed in, separates the remaining props, keeps a pressed state synced from a selected prop, and renders a native button with type button, aria-pressed, disabled, aria-label from accessibilityLabel, and handlers for click (toggles and calls onPressedChange and onClick), focus and blur. Child spans are marked by data-element; the decorative icon is aria-hidden and its glyph is set through a CSS variable.

YAML promoted-primitive mapping for a Text component: keyed by component name, with elementType (Figma layer type, text) and a map list. Each entry has a source (typography, textColor, layoutSizingHorizontal, content) and either a values dictionary from Figma style or enum name to a prop/value object, or a single prop target (content maps to the text prop).

Before/after composition code: before, nested divs and spans with inline flex, gap, padding, colour and font styles that reference token variables; after, nested Layout components with direction, itemSpacing and padding props, and Title and Text components with size, colour and text props.

rules.rule: Fit the code to the contract, not the catalog: generators key off what a spec declares, never one library's own conventions or quirks.
Map state props to shared state concepts (hover, active, disabled) explicitly, so each team's naming (state=pressed, isDisabled) translates directly and code can style interactions between states.
Generated state CSS uses real pseudo-classes, and hover rules exclude disabled and aria-disabled, so disabled takes precedence over hover.
Give each interactive anatomy element a role. Without one, generators emit markup that looks right but does nothing (a div button that cannot be focused or clicked; a checkbox with no input).

From a role, generate the platform's native control, the accessibility wiring between elements, and the event handlers in the contract. One togglebutton annotation produced aria-pressed, a pressed state and a click toggle on a native button.
A role implies a contract of expected props. For a text input: onChange, onBlur, onFocus, onKeyDown, name, autocomplete, value.
The generator must handle precedence between roles, states and actions, and how they compose.
Type props as one enum per multi-value prop, an interface built from those enums, and a single defaults constant that is merged under the props passed in.
An accessible name is a prop (accessibilityLabel) mapped to aria-label; decorative parts such as icons are aria-hidden.
Components and generated CSS reference tokens as CSS custom properties (semantic names such as action-hover or text-primary), emitted library-wide together with their modes.

Promote primitive layers (frames, text, glyphs) that match a mapping into core system components (Layout, Text, Heading, Eyebrow, Icon) with prop settings, so composition code stays on-system and has no inline styles.
Treat generated scaffolds as a regenerable baseline: script the contracts, style sheets and scaffolds first; agents and humans polish to production grade at the end of the line.
Keep scripting until scripting a thing costs more than the benefit of being able to regenerate it.
Check generated output with visual regression: compare each Storybook story with Figma images and burn down each library's defects (start, fix-loop, end QA skills) until it runs green.
Generate Storybook stories (variants, examples, sticker sheet) straight from the spec; they double as visual checks of foundations, primitives, nested configuration, layout and slot composition.
Generate code to harden the spec format: a generator cannot ask what you meant, so undocumented conventions surface and must move into the schema and the generator logic.

terms.meaning: Curtis's tooling (specsplugin.com) that extracts structured component specs from Figma. Its commands include fetch, generate, react and webcomponents.
The spec acting as the component's contract, on which code is built. In output, contract.ts is the typed surface: prop enums, an interface and defaults.
The governing principle: generators follow what specs declare, not the quirks of a particular library.
A pipeline that consumes specs and scripts most code (contracts, styles, scaffolds) up front, with agents or humans polishing at the end.
The generated renderable component, meant to be duplicated and evolved instead of edited in place.
Library-wide state ideas (hover, active, disabled) mapped to whatever Figma prop and value express them.

articles.title: Component and Part Roles as Composites of Behavior and Accessibility
articles.thesis: Figma specs carry visuals and prop enums but not behaviour or accessibility, so generated code looks right and does nothing. Curtis proposes a "role": one word, annotated on a component root or part, that bundles many behaviour and accessibility obligations (element, keyboard, announcement, name, callbacks, state handling, native states) the way a typography token bundles font values. Each platform translates the role natively; the spec records intent, not implementation. A small vocabulary (100-150 role uses per 50-component catalog) suffices.

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Human name of the component (e.g. Favorite button). Top-level key of the spec.
spec_structure.quote: title: Favorite button

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Map of named elements (root plus parts such as icon, formLabel, container, value, errorMessage). Each element is an object.
spec_structure.quote: the role property per annotated anatomy element

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Structural kind of the element, e.g. container or glyph.
spec_structure.quote: type: container

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Optional role from the roles vocabulary: a control role on the root/control element, or a part role on a sub-part. Declares intent (behaviour), distinct from the name (identity).
spec_structure.quote: A role declares intent, how a component or part behaves.

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Props come from the Figma component property design and keep their Figma names (e.g. selected, disabled, readOnly, validation enum, value, placeholder). Roles wire to these names rather than imposing new ones. Not shown as an explicit spec block in the article.
spec_structure.quote: roles wire to the names you include on the asset

spec_structure.what_it_holds: Visual states (hover, disabled, active, validation) mapped from Figma prop enums to CSS; generators connect roles with these existing state conventions. Exact spec shape not shown.
spec_structure.quote: connects roles with existing states conventions

spec_structure.section_or_field: Figma Dev Mode annotation (alternate input surface)
spec_structure.what_it_holds: The same role can be declared as a Dev Mode annotation on a layer, e.g. role:togglebutton on root and role:indicator on icon. Either the annotation or the spec field is sufficient input.
spec_structure.quote: In Figma, a role is a Dev Mode annotation applied to the layer.

examples: Spec YAML for a Favorite button: a title string, then an anatomy map with two keys (root, icon); each value is an object with a type string (container / glyph) and a role string (togglebutton / indicator). Two levels of nesting, all string values.

React output without roles: a styled div wrapping a span icon, no interactivity. With roles: a native button with type=button, aria-pressed bound to state, onClick handler, and the icon span marked aria-hidden.

Full generated React FavoriteButton function: internal pressed state initialised from the selected prop and re-synced whenever the prop changes (prop wins); a toggle handler that flips state and calls an optional onPressedChange callback; renders a button with className, aria-pressed, disabled from prop, onClick; decorative icon aria-hidden.

Web Components (Lit-style) render method returning a button with aria-pressed and a slot, with a comment noting a label in another component cannot reference the button by id across the shadow boundary.
SwiftUI sketch: a Toggle bound to a boolean, styled as a button, containing a heart image.
Jetpack Compose sketch: IconToggleButton with checked and onCheckedChange, containing an Icon with null contentDescription.

TextInput React without roles: nested divs with BEM classNames and data-element attributes (root, formLabel, container, value, errorMessage), a data-validation attribute, and an error message rendered only when validation equals error.

TextInput React with roles: generated ids via useId for the control, the label description and the error message; controlled value state re-synced from prop; root carries data-disabled / data-read-only / data-validation; a composed FormLabel receives htmlFor and descriptionId; a native input (type text) carries id, value, onChange (updates state and calls prop callback), placeholder, disabled, readOnly, aria-invalid only when in error, aria-describedby joining description id and error id when in error, onBlur; composed FormErrorMessage receives the error id and renders only on error.

rules.rule: Separate identity from intent: a component name says what it is called; a role says how it behaves. Do not overload names to carry behaviour, and do not let generators infer behaviour from layer names (FavoriteButton, MuteButton, Bookmark, Bold are all togglebutton without the word toggle).
Annotate roles on the component root and/or the relevant parts; about half of components need none, most others need up to three; a complex field like TextInput needs around seven.

A control role (e.g. togglebutton) must expand to: a real native element, focus and keyboard operation (Enter and Space), correct announcement (aria-pressed), an accessible name from a visible or accessibility label, a change callback prop plus click handler, state that starts from the prop, follows prop changes and flips on interaction, native disabled as a real attribute, correct hover/focus wiring, and resetting browser default styles.
State pattern for stateful roles: internal state is seeded from the prop and the prop wins whenever it changes; the callback is optional so the component works uncontrolled.
Emit required state attributes even when false (aria-pressed=false), because omitting it makes a toggle announce as a plain button.
Decorative indicator parts (icons, check glyphs, switch thumbs) are hidden from assistive tech when the control's state already conveys the meaning.
Generators should use prop names already chosen in the design asset (e.g. selected) rather than imposing their own.
When an obligation cannot be met from the inputs (e.g. icon-only button with no label), the generator or agent should warn that a label is owed rather than invent one.

On web, only emit role attribute values that are legal ARIA roles; non-ARIA vocabulary names (togglebutton, disclosure, errormessage, indicator, value) must translate to native elements/attributes instead, since an unknown role is discarded and leaves no semantics.

No platform's translation is the source of truth; the spec records what the element is and each platform (web, React, Web Components, SwiftUI, Compose) maps it to its native control. This is what makes a role a contract.

Part wiring for fields: label becomes a real label tied to the control's id; errormessage text is associated with the control (aria-describedby) and aria-invalid set only while the error renders; description ids also feed aria-describedby.
The textbox role must sit on the layer that becomes the native input, which may require restructuring design layers so border and padding land correctly.
Drop design-tool-only props that the platform handles natively (e.g. a placeholder-visible boolean, since an input shows placeholder when empty), ideally during the design-to-spec transform.
Roles should be authored on a shared surface: designers declare, engineers and accessibility specialists review or extend, agents may propose roles in bulk for experts to confirm.
Role bundles are not design decisions and should be identical across design systems; tokens, radius, iconography and prop names may differ.
Check each generator's role emission for completeness and accuracy against multiple design libraries; interactions between roles needed adjustment in testing.

terms.meaning: A one-word annotation on a component root or part declaring behavioural and accessibility intent; a composite that expands to many obligations per platform.
A named bundle of related decisions applied as a whole, like typography or shadow composite tokens; roles apply this idea to behaviour and accessibility.
Answers what an element is. Named: togglebutton, textbox, disclosure, button, link, checkbox, radio, switch, slider, spinbutton, textarea, password, searchbox, group, alert, status, progressbar.
Answers which part of a control an element serves. Named: label, errormessage, indicator, description, value, placeholder, panel, increment, decrement.
Name declares identity; role declares intent/behaviour.
The spec's map of a component's named elements, each with a type and optional role.
Curtis's Figma-to-spec toolkit, whose docs hold the role inventory; it includes react and webcomponents generators (experimental).
The spec records what an element is, independent of any platform's implementation; each platform answers with its native control.
Figma's annotation feature used as the design-side surface for declaring roles (e.g. role:togglebutton).

warnings: Figma cannot express behaviour or accessibility: pixel-perfect generated code may be a div that cannot be clicked, focused or announced.
Supplemental written requirements docs cover some but not all behaviour and accessibility details.
Inferring behaviour from layer names fails: many toggle components have no 'toggle' in their name.

Accessibility annotation sticker kits name parts but miss the larger pattern, are easily missed, and force hand re-implementation; headless libraries bundle behaviour but only in code, disconnected from design.
Omitting aria-pressed when false silently drops the control's meaning.
Emitting a non-ARIA role name on web is worse than emitting none.
Web Components: id-based label-to-control references do not cross the shadow boundary; Curtis says this is unsolved in his toolkit and the browser fix is experimental.
Native iOS/Android generators are not built; his mappings are suggestions from agents, unverified.
Layer structure sometimes must change for the role to land on the right element (textbox on the input layer).
One role (textbox) unfolds into about seven obligations; interactions among roles needed adjustment, generators may be imperfect and must be checked for completeness and accuracy.
Design-only props (placeholder visible boolean) should not survive into code.
Dialogs, menus, tabs and comboboxes are not yet in the role inventory; the vocabulary is incomplete and he does not plan to complete its long tail.
The post began as an AI draft, which the author discloses.
gaps: No full spec schema is given: only title and anatomy (type, role) are shown. Props, variants, states, tokens, layout, content and keyboard maps are not specified as spec sections; props/states appear only implicitly via Figma props and generated code.
Prop typing and defaults are not formally defined; only implied by code (selected defaults to false via nullish fallback, value to empty string, optional callbacks).
No keyboard interaction tables beyond Enter/Space for togglebutton.

Tabs, DropdownMenu (menu) and Dialog are explicitly not covered yet; for those three of the lead's five components the article offers no role design. Button (button/togglebutton) and Input (textbox with label, description, errormessage, placeholder, value) are covered.
The 'action' composite (e.g. dismiss, clear) is mentioned as future work with no detail.
The full role inventory lives in external Specs plugin docs, which were not fetched.

Article sections covered: intro, A role is a composite, How roles work (What you declare, What it generates), The roles vocabulary (Controls, Parts, Where role names come from), How roles generalize in systems (For teammates collaborating, Across platforms, Across design systems), Example: Text Input's many parts, Where could roles go? articles.title: What Component Specs Leave Behind
articles.thesis: A component contract (spec) should carry design intent as exhaustively as needed, and the way to test that is a round trip: generate a spec from a Figma component, render the spec back into Figma, regenerate a spec, and diff. Shallow contracts round-trip cleanly only because they carry little. The diff will not converge to zero; success is converging on named sets: confirmed assumptions, defects to fix, and what the contract cannot, will not, or does not yet carry.

Inline notation only: variantDepth with integer values 1, 2 and 9999, meaning how many variant axes are compared in combination (1 = each axis alone, 2 = every pair, 9999 = all combinations).

Inline variant axis examples: a boolean axis selected with values true|false and an enum axis state with values rest|hover|pressed, used to show that styling can change only when two values co-occur (selected true AND hover).
Inline enum figmaKey with values NONE, SENTENCE, TITLE declaring the casing designers use for names in Figma.

rules.rule: Aim for lossless transformation from design asset to spec: nothing dropped, altered or invented.
When a token is bound, the spec must record the token, never the resolved raw value.
Capture how styling and layer presence change across combinations of variant axes, not just each axis alone; he evaluates all combinations (variantDepth 9999).
States are expressed as variant axes (e.g. state rest/hover/pressed, selected true/false); interactions between axes must be recorded where they change styling or presence.
Do not collapse a BOOLEAN and a SLOT prop into one nullable slot if the layer is only bound as a slot in some variants; preserve per-variant prop binding.
Record when a part is customizable per variant (e.g. an Alert icon fixed in the error variant, customizable in neutral).
Record how padding and other values differ depending on whether content is a composable slot or a built-in label.
Preserve authored order; alphabetical sorting is not neutral and destroys it.
Booleans must be typed as booleans everywhere, including variant options spelled true/True/false/False.
Hidden layers still exist and must be carried; visibility is not existence.
Names must round-trip losslessly; converting labels to camelCase or snake_case is lossy, so keep a safe key grammar and the original design-tool name.
Test a contract by round trip: generate baseline spec, render to Figma, generate test spec, diff, report, delete the test asset; loop until the diff is residue you can name.
Prefer a deterministic script (no AI) for spec-to-asset rendering; agentic generation would likely be lossy and error-prone.
Have the report step separate unimplemented features from defects and regressions, group symptoms into root-cause themes and file prioritised issues.
A model change caused by a fix (e.g. a misnamed property) gets an ADR, not just a code fix.
State openly what the contract cannot, does not yet, and will not carry, and tell consumers.
Emit warnings when the generator cannot resolve or bind something, rather than failing silently.

terms.meaning: Markdown and/or JSON data describing a UI component, generated from a Figma asset and consumed by agents and engineers.
Converting data between structures without losing, altering or inventing information.
Intent dropped, mangled or invented during design-to-spec conversion, which then compounds downstream.
How much intent a contract carries (variant combinations, nesting, slots, content, props).
Setting for how many variant axes are compared in combination; 1 per axis, 2 pairwise, 9999 all.
Generate spec from asset, render spec back to asset, regenerate and diff to measure loss.
His Specs tool's Figma-to-spec transform.
His deterministic script that builds a Figma component from a spec in seconds.
The author's own spec tool; Classic was the first generation with a two-way (pairwise variant) feature.
Orchestrating script plus a Figma plugin bridge connecting Figma, the LLM chat and cached library data (variables, icons, assets).
Convention NONE|SENTENCE|TITLE declaring how designers case names in Figma.
A prop existing in code but not in the Figma component.

warnings: Shallow contracts round-trip perfectly but are misleading: an empty diff only proves the little that was carried survived.
Most tools go no deeper than pairwise variant comparison, missing intent expressed in deeper combinations.
Complex intent (per-variant customizability, slot-vs-label padding, partial slot binding) is the easiest to lose and hardest to spot in visual review; the contract had no place for it.
Reading a schema shows what it meant to model, not what a spec actually carried.
Visual review and even visual regression snapshots miss data defects such as slot content marked fixed width when it fills.
Rarely used properties without unit tests or fixtures can silently never work (clipsContent defined as clipContent).
Case conversion of names to camelCase/snake_case is lossy.

Cannot be carried via Figma's plugin API: custom order of non-VARIANT props in the Props panel (which carries priority and grouping intent), and both width and height variable bindings under locked aspect ratio.
Not yet supported: Grid autolayout, unusual line end styles, stacked strokes and fills.
Won't be supported: Figma motion data, judged too costly and rarely used.
Converging the diff to zero is the wrong goal; aim to name the remaining gaps.
gaps: All article headings are covered: intro, Loss, Depth, The round trip, Starting in reverse, The loop, The Reckoning, Expose assumptions, Fix the transformation, Expand the schema, What can't be supported, What isn't yet supported, What won't be supported.

No concrete schema or field list is given. The model elements (components, anatomy, props, styling, bindings, variants, slots, nested composition, code-only props, examples) are named in one sentence without structure.
Accessibility is not mentioned at all: no ARIA roles, keyboard behaviour, focus or contrast.
No role assignment for parts beyond named layers.
Prop defaults are not discussed. Typing appears only as Figma prop kinds plus boolean consistency and nullable slots.
Content/voice guidance, behaviours/interaction logic and responsive layout rules are not covered, except layout fill-vs-fixed for slot content.
Spec-to-code generation is not described. The only generator target is Figma (the render command); code is said to be consumed by agents and engineers. Docs generation is not described.
Token structure, naming or W3C DTCG format is not discussed beyond requiring bound tokens, not hex values.

Tools named: the author's Specs (generate, render, report skill), Specs Classic, a Figma plugin bridge, GitHub issues, ADRs, unit tests/fixtures, visual regression snapshots, and Addy Osmani's Loop Engineering writings as inspiration. No third-party spec or codegen tools are named.

sections.heading: Brand accent: Pink
sections.content: Chai chose Pink as brand accent on Nov 16: Pink 800 in light, Pink 700 or 600 in dark. Author recommends Pink 600 in dark because Pink 700 blends into dark surfaces. repo.token_pipeline:
Script: scripts/build-tokens.mjs. buildCss() reads tokens/souvenir.tokens.json and writes dist/tokens.css, the only output it makes. scripts/build.mjs then concatenates dist/tokens.css + src/base/*.css + src/components/*/*.css into dist/souvenir.css and dist/souvenir.min.css. It also writes dist/components/<name>.css and .js, and dist/souvenir.js.

Values: a primitive is written as a literal. Colours are written as oklch(L C H). Every semantic and component token is written as var() of its alias target, so the CSS keeps the alias chain.

Naming, from cssName(path):
- primitive: '--sv-p-' + rest joined by '-'
- semantic: '--sv-' + rest, with the theme segment (light or dark) dropped
- component: '--sv-' + rest, with the word 'component' dropped
Examples:
- primitive.neutral.22 -> --sv-p-neutral-22
- primitive.accent.blue -> --sv-p-accent-blue
- semantic.light.color.text-soft -> --sv-color-text-soft
- semantic.space.4 -> --sv-space-4
- component.button.primary-fill -> --sv-button-primary-fill (= var(--sv-color-accent))
Also: component.field.error-edge-width -> --sv-field-error-edge-width.

File structure: the file opens with '@layer sv.tokens, sv.base, sv.components;'. Everything sits inside @layer sv.tokens.

Themes:
- :root {color-scheme: light; every token}.
- Dark redeclares only the semantic.dark.color keys whose $value differs from light. It does so twice: in '@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) {...} }' and in ':root[data-theme="dark"] {...}'.
- A component colour aliases semantic.light.color.<key>. The resolver's themed() reads that as "the active theme's key". In the CSS it is simply var(--sv-color-<key>), which the theme blocks re-point.

Accent: there is one re-point block per non-default key of primitive.accent, emitted last: ':root[data-accent="teal"] { --sv-color-accent: var(--sv-p-accent-teal); }'. The default is whatever semantic.light.color.accent aliases (blue). buildCss throws if an accent block precedes the dark block, or if dark redeclares the accent.

The page sets the attributes: an inline theme script in the head maps ?theme=light|dark to html[data-theme] and ?accent=blue|teal to html[data-accent].

repo.component_conventions: Files: src/components//.css, plus an optional .js. Docs: docs/components/.md (markup to copy plus an option/state table). Demo page: screens/demo-.html. CSS: - Everything sits inside '@layer sv.components { }' (lint css-layer). - Selectors must start from .sv- and may target only .sv- and .sv-__, where is the folder name (css-selector-scope). - Values come only from var(--sv-...) semantic or component tokens. Only logical properties are allowed. - Raw lengths are limited to 0, 100%, 50% and 1fr, plus cqi inside clamp() or min(). - @media is limited to min-width 48rem, prefers-reduced-motion, prefers-color-scheme and forced-colors. System colours are allowed only inside forced-colors: active. Naming, as a block with __parts: - .sv-field, .sv-field__label, .sv-field__hint, .sv-field__error, .sv-field__control - .sv-button has no parts Options are data attributes on the root, matched by attribute selectors: - button: data-variant="secondary|primary|quiet", data-width="full" - base.css: data-gap, data-layout="split", data-align, data-row="total" and others States use native attributes, ARIA and pseudo-classes, never state classes: - .sv-button: :hover:not(:disabled,[data-variant="quiet"]), :active:not(:disabled), :focus-visible, :disabled, [aria-busy="true"] (adds a ::before mask of var(--sv-icon-busy), turning under prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) - .sv-field__control: [readonly] (dashed edge), :disabled (thin edge, soft text; the label goes soft via .sv-field:has(.sv-field__control:disabled) .sv-field__label), [aria-invalid="true"] (border-inline-start var(--sv-field-error-edge-width) in var(--sv-color-danger)) - .sv-field__error::before uses the danger mask, so the error is never shown by colour alone - [hidden] is handled once in base.css with display:none !important Scripts are light-DOM custom elements that wrap plain, working markup, with no shadow DOM and no styles. Each is guarded by `if (!customElements.get(...)) customElements.define(...)`. setup() runs in connectedCallback, with a MutationObserver fallback when children arrive late. -

css-selector-scope: in a component file, a selector that targets an id, a class other than .sv-<folder> or .sv-<folder>__part, or that does not start from that class

html-inline-svg: an inline <svg>

repo.contrast_rules:
In scripts/check-tokens.mjs, runChecks(doc) uses the inner helper colour(theme, accent, key). It resolves semantic.<theme>.color.<key> via build-tokens resolve(doc, path, {theme, accent}) and returns OKLCH components. contrastOklch from scripts/lib/color.mjs gives the WCAG ratio.

The array RULES inside runChecks sets the pairs and minimums:
- text-contrast, min 7: text on ground, text on panel, text on well
- text-soft-contrast, min 4.5: text-soft on ground, text-soft on panel, text-soft on well
- on-accent, min 4.5: on-solid on accent
- on-status, min 3: on-solid on danger, warning, success, neutral-solid
- boundary-contrast, min 3: each of accent, edge, focus, danger, warning, success, neutral-solid against panel and against ground, plus edge against well
- inverse-contrast, min 7: on-inverse on inverse
- inverse-boundary, min 3: inverse against panel and against ground

Every rule runs for both THEMES (light, dark). A pair involving 'accent' is measured once per key of primitive.accent (blue, teal); other pairs are measured once per theme.

Further colour rules:
- focus-equals-text: focus must resolve to the same components as text in each theme.
- solids-same: accent, danger, warning and success must have identical $value in light and dark.
- status-hue: each primitive.status.* hue must be at least 30 degrees (hueDistance) from each primitive.accent.* hue.

All key names are hardcoded: COLOR_KEYS, SAME_IN_BOTH, and the literal keys in RULES.

Separately, scripts/check-screens.mjs measures rendered contrast:
- text: 4.5:1, or 3:1 at 24px and above
- control boundary: 3:1 for the best border or fill
- focus outline: 3:1
It uses relativeLuminance and contrastRatio from lib/color.mjs after verifying them against 21:1 and 3.03:1 at start.
repo.screens_pipeline:
Serving: scripts/serve.mjs exports createServer({root, port, host}). It is a static server for the repo root with Cache-Control no-store, answers GET and HEAD only (anything else gets 405), and serves index.html for a directory. Standalone it runs as `npm run serve` on port 4174 at 127.0.0.1; the commit history shows a launch entry for it. check-screens and check-noscript call createServer({port: 0}), which picks a random free port.

Browser: playwright-core chromium.launch, headless. The executable is searched in this order: PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM, playwright-core's own path, then cached ms-playwright revisions. If none is found it runs `npx playwright-core install chromium`.

Per state: a new context with viewport {width, 800}, deviceScaleFactor 1 and colorScheme set to the theme. The URL is `${base}/screens/<file>?theme=light|dark`; the screen check never passes ?accent. The script waits for fonts.ready, evaluates PAGE_LIB, measures, presses Tab through up to 300 stops, then takes a fullPage screenshot with animations: 'disabled'.

Where pictures go:
- Full run: digests/2026-11-15/screens/<path-with-dashes>-<width>-<theme>.png and data in gates/raw/2026-11-15-screens.json. Both dates are hardcoded constants.
- --only: scripts/.tmp/check-screens-only/screens/ and screens.json.
- --dir: scripts/.tmp/check-screens-out/, or --out.

Theme and accent in a page: the inline head script maps ?theme=light|dark to data-theme and ?accent=blue|teal to data-accent. Without it the theme follows prefers-color-scheme. Accent pictures in the digest (digests/2026-11-15/accent/*-blue|teal-*.png) come from scripts/shots-accent.mjs, which was not opened.
agents_md_promises: Read in order: AGENTS.md, docs/layout.md, docs/patterns.md, then docs/components/<name>.md. The notes are the contract; do not read src/ or copy from other screens.
Rule 1: a screen has no style of its own: no <style>, no style attribute, no inline SVG; every class or custom element begins sv-.
Rule 2: never invent: use only the classes, options and values the notes name; build with what exists and report what was missing.
Rule 3: text is ink: you cannot colour text.
Rule 4: at most one primary button per screen, for the action that commits (pays, sends, changes); a form-only page's submit is the primary.
Rule 5: a status is never colour alone: use message or status with data-tone.
Rule 6: everything works without script: a real <form> with method and action; navigation is <a> (it may be a.sv-button); every <button> has a type; type=button only where a note names its script.
Rule 7: every control has a visible label; no placeholder as label.
Rule 8: headings in order: one h1, then h2, then h3.
Rule 9: text a person typed, shown as text, goes in an element with data-user-content.
Rule 10: an amount is never styled text: a total goes in a cost-summary, a list amount in the list's trail.
Which-part table: layout classes, sv-list, button, field, select, checkbox, cost-summary, error-summary, message, status, chat-message, proposal.
An irreversible action gets its own page, with no dialog; machine-written text gets a warning message beside it.
Not yet in the system: tabs, dialog, toast, table, date picker, radio, navigation, pagination, images, avatars, icons beyond the tone marks.

Words: plain full sentences; no exclamation marks, please, sorry or oops; verb-plus-object button labels; errors that say what to do; Souvenir says I, we only for service failures; date, time and money formats; no-break spaces; never claim what did not happen.
Theme follows the device; ?theme=light|dark and ?accent=teal are handled by the page skeleton.

Check your work: save in screens/ and run node scripts/build.mjs, node scripts/lint.mjs, node scripts/check-screens.mjs --only <name>, then look at the screenshots; done when both find nothing; npm run check runs everything.

hard_to_reuse: cssName() in build-tokens.mjs drops the layer name for semantic and component tokens. A new component group named like a semantic group (color, space, size, font, border, focus, duration, radius) would build to a clashing --sv-<group>-* name. unique-css-names catches this, so it fails loudly. The five new component names must avoid those words.

The prefixes are hardcoded: '--sv-p-' for primitives and '--sv-' for everything else in cssName. The lint's css-var-prefix forbids primitives by that prefix, not by layer. If v2 renames the primitive prefix, the 'components never read primitives' rule silently stops working until the lint is changed.

build-tokens.mjs hardwires the theme and accent model: THEMES=['light','dark'], themed() (only semantic.<theme>.color.* is theme-switched), the accent override in resolve() (semantic.*.color.accent -> primitive.accent.<k>), buildCss reading semantic.light.color.accent and primitive.accent, and the dark-block and accent-block CSS selectors.

check-tokens.mjs hardcodes token names: COLOR_KEYS (16 required keys such as ground, panel, well, text, text-soft, edge, on-solid, focus, inverse, neutral-solid), SAME_IN_BOTH, every pair key in RULES, focus-equals-text, the status-hue paths primitive.status and primitive.accent, and TOP layer names. The component-color-slot rule forces component colours to alias semantic.light.color.<key>. A differently named token set means rewriting these lists and the 25 fixtures, whose patch paths name today's tokens.

lint.mjs hardcodes: CHECKED_DATA (11 data attributes), SCRIPT_DATA_PREFIX /^data-(error|busy)-/, THEME_SCRIPT_STRINGS (includes 'blue' and 'teal', so a third accent needs a lint edit), the 'sv-' class and element prefix, 'sv-button' and 'sv-checkbox' literals, the dist/souvenir.css and dist/souvenir.js paths, and DOC_FILES.
css-selector-scope ties the folder name to the class: src/components/<name>/ may only target .sv-<name> and .sv-<name>__*. A new component's folder, class and token group must share one name.

check-screens.mjs PAGE_LIB has component-specific rules and selectors: .sv-cost-summary and its __row[data-row=total] dd (cost-total-largest, total-below-first-screen), .sv-chat-message and its __from, .sv-proposal, .sv-status[data-tone=busy], .sv-message[data-tone=success], a.sv-button, and the --sv-color-accent custom property (many-accent-fills).
